text:
A plant that can poison you is being used as a fence by millions of farmers. And the fence is also dinner.

Read that again.

In parts of Indonesia, a farmer can build a barrier around an entire field for roughly the price of a few afternoons of labor. No steel. No concrete. No wire shipped from a factory three islands away.

He uses sticks. Dead-looking sticks, cut from the last harvest. He pushes them into the dirt.

Then the sticks wake up.

Within weeks they sprout leaves. Within months they are a green wall. And within a year, hidden under that wall, they are quietly growing something you can eat, sell, grind into flour, boil into snacks or turn into the pearls at the bottom of your bubble tea.

This is the story of the strangest security system in agriculture. It has a body count in its history, a conspiracy of chemistry in its leaves, and a plot twist that most people who eat it have never heard.

Let's go. Thread-length, no filler. Buckle up.

---

1. THE PLANT THAT SHOULD NOT BE FOOD

Let's start with the uncomfortable part.

Cassava (Manihot esculenta) is loaded with a defensive chemical system. Its tissues contain compounds called cyanogenic glycosides, mainly linamarin and a close cousin called lotaustralin.

Here's the trick. In the living, undamaged plant, these compounds sit in one compartment of the cell. A separate enzyme, linamarase, sits in another. Nothing happens. Peace.

Now let something bite the plant. Chew it. Crush it. Tear it.

The walls break. The compounds meet the enzyme. And the reaction releases hydrogen cyanide.

Yes. That cyanide.

The plant doesn't carry poison around like a loaded gun. It carries a bomb with two separate ingredients, and it lets the attacker mix them by trying to eat it.

That is not a bug. That is the entire design. Cassava evolved this system for one purpose: to make whoever takes a bite regret it.

And humans looked at this plant and decided: yes, this will be our staple crop.

---

2. THE NUMBER THAT BREAKS YOUR BRAIN

Cassava is one of the most important food crops on Earth. Hundreds of millions of people depend on it for daily calories, especially across Africa, Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America.

It is not a hobby crop. It is not a niche superfood. It is infrastructure.

Think about the logic of that for a second.

A plant with built-in chemical weapons became a lifeline for a significant fraction of humanity.

Why? Because cassava does what almost nothing else does.

It grows in poor soil where other crops give up.
It tolerates drought that flattens maize.
It survives neglect that would destroy a delicate crop.
It can sit in the ground, unharvested, as a living pantry, for a long stretch of time when conditions allow, instead of rotting on a deadline like most vegetables.

Farmers call crops like this insurance. Cassava is insurance with a toxic personality.

---

3. THE LONG JOURNEY NOBODY TALKS ABOUT

Cassava is not even from Asia.

Its origin story points to South America, where people domesticated it thousands of years ago. It is a New World plant.

It reached Southeast Asia much later, carried along colonial trade routes after European ships began stitching the continents together. It then did something remarkable: it conquered the tropics.

In Indonesia, especially across Java and other islands, cassava became a backbone food, a famine buffer, and a cultural fixture. Over time it picked up local names and local dishes, and it became so normal that many people forget it was ever foreign.

Today Indonesia sits among the major cassava-producing nations of the world. A plant that began on another continent became so woven into Indonesian farming that it is practically part of the landscape.

Which brings us to the thing that should not work, but does.

---

4. THE FENCE THAT GROWS ITSELF

Most crops are planted from seeds.

Cassava, in practice, is usually planted from sticks.

Farmers cut mature stems into sections, each with several nodes, the little knuckles along the stem. They stick them into the ground, upright or at an angle. Roots form at the nodes. Shoots form at the nodes.

A piece of dead-looking wood becomes a new plant.

No seed. No nursery. No expensive input. The crop is, quite literally, cloning itself from its own body.

Now notice what that means.

If you can plant a stick and it becomes a plant, you can plant a lot of sticks, close together, in a line.

And what do you get?

A wall.

Not a metaphorical wall. A real, physical, thickening barrier, built from the same raw material you already have piled up behind the barn after harvest.

The farmer isn't buying a fence. He's growing one.

Fences in farming are expensive in a way people who have never farmed don't appreciate. Posts, wire, nails, labor, repairs, replacements. A fence is a recurring bill. It rusts. It sags. It gets cut. It needs to be rebuilt.

A living fence does the reverse. It repairs itself. It gets denser over time. And if you plant it right, it pays you back.

---

5. WHAT THE FENCE IS ACTUALLY FOR

Here is where honest storytelling matters, because the internet loves a magical claim.

A living cassava barrier is not a force field. It is not a guaranteed shield against every animal on Earth. Nothing in farming is that clean.

But it does several jobs at once, and the combination is the point.

First, a physical boundary. Dense stems and foliage make a field harder to casually walk into. Loose livestock, wandering animals and opportunistic foragers meet resistance before they meet the crop.

Second, a chemical hint. Cassava's leaves and stems carry that cyanogenic chemistry, and bitter varieties carry more of it. Animals that nibble learn quickly that not everything green is friendly. Many farmers rely on exactly that reputation.

Third, a visual and territorial marker. A planted line says: this is claimed ground.

Fourth, wind protection. A tall, leafy row can soften wind across a field and reduce the damage it does to young plants.

Fifth, a soil anchor. Roots help hold edges together where rain would otherwise wash soil away.

And sixth, the one that makes the whole thing genius.

The fence is a crop.

---

6. THE PLOT TWIST: YOUR FENCE IS A BANK ACCOUNT

Think like a farmer on a small plot.

Every square meter matters. Every meter of border you give up to a non-productive barrier is land that earns nothing. A normal fence consumes money to build and produces nothing in return.

A cassava border does something almost unfair.

It protects the field AND it grows tubers. The thing guarding the harvest is also part of the harvest.

That changes the math completely. Instead of a cost center, the perimeter becomes an asset. Instead of a wall you maintain, you have a wall you eventually eat.

It is like hiring a security guard who also cooks your lunch and doesn't ask for a salary.

And it gets better. Cassava leaves themselves are food in Indonesia. Young leaves are cooked, after proper preparation, into dishes eaten across the country. The same plant that is a fence, a root crop and a flour source is also a leafy vegetable.

One stick. Four jobs. That is not a farming trick. That is systems design.

---

7. WHY THIS IS SMARTER THAN IT LOOKS

Most people look at a living fence and think: low tech.

Look again. It is high strategy built on low cost.

Consider what a farmer in a tight-margin environment actually needs: something cheap, something local, something that doesn't depend on a supply chain, something that survives mistakes, something that keeps working when money runs short.

A cassava barrier ticks every box.

The material is already on the farm.
The skill is already in the family.
The maintenance is mostly pruning and replanting a gap.
The failure mode is soft: a patch dies, you stick in another cutting.

Compare that with a manufactured fence, where one broken section can leave the whole line open until someone buys and installs a replacement.

Resilience isn't about being the strongest. It's about degrading gracefully. Living systems do that. Hardware usually doesn't.

---

8. THE DARK SIDE: THE PLANT THAT HAS HURT PEOPLE

I promised you the part with stakes. Here it is.

Cassava is only safe when it is prepared correctly. This is not a footnote. It is the central fact of the whole crop.

Bitter varieties, which carry higher levels of cyanogenic compounds, must be processed: peeled, grated, soaked, fermented, dried, cooked, often several of these together. Done properly, the toxic compounds break down and escape, and the food becomes safe and nutritious.

Done badly, or rushed, especially when people are under pressure from hunger, drought or war, the consequences can be severe.

There is a recognized disease linked to heavy reliance on insufficiently processed bitter cassava, particularly where diets are narrow and protein is scarce. It is called konzo, and it causes sudden, permanent paralysis of the legs. It has been documented in parts of Africa.

Let that sink in. The same plant that feeds hundreds of millions has, in the wrong conditions, crippled people.

This is why traditional processing knowledge is not folklore. It is survival technology, refined over generations. Every step of grating, soaking and drying exists because someone, long ago, figured out what happens if you skip it.

And that is exactly why a cassava fence is fascinating. The farmers using it live inside a culture that already understands this plant deeply. They know which varieties are for the fence line, which are for the pot, how to cut, how to plant and how to process. The knowledge is the real fence.

---

9. THE MANY LIVES OF A ROOT

Once processed, cassava turns into one of the most flexible ingredients on the planet.

Boil it, and you have a starchy side dish.
Fry it into crisp chips, a snack sold from roadside stalls to supermarket shelves.
Steam and mash it into sweet treats.
Ferment it into tangy traditional foods.
Dry it into a shelf-stable form that can sit in storage when fresh roots would spoil.
Extract the starch and you get tapioca.

Yes, tapioca. Those chewy pearls in bubble tea started as the root of a plant with a chemical defense system.

Cassava starch also shows up in industry: in food processing, in adhesives, in textiles, in packaging materials, even as a feedstock in bio-based products. A farmer's border row connects, through a long chain, to factories and cafes around the world.

A stick in the dirt in a field on the other side of the planet. Possibly in your drink.

---

10. THE CLOCK THAT RUNS ON CASSAVA

Here is a detail that explains a lot of cassava culture.

Fresh cassava roots do not last long once harvested. They begin to deteriorate quickly, often within a few days. That is an enormous problem for a food people depend on.

So humans solved it in two ways.

One: leave the roots in the ground until you need them. The field itself becomes the storage unit.

Two: process the roots fast into forms that last, such as dried chips and flour.

This is why you see such a rich variety of cassava foods. It is not culinary decoration. It is a preservation strategy wearing a delicious disguise.

And it is also why a cassava border is quietly brilliant. A farmer can leave part of the plant working as a living barrier while it continues to develop a reserve underground. The fence is guarding the field and storing food at the same time.

---

11. WHAT ECONOMISTS WOULD CALL THIS

If you handed this arrangement to a consultant, they would charge a lot of money to give it a name.

Multifunctional landscape design. Agroforestry-adjacent boundary planting. Integrated low-input risk management. Circular resource use.

The farmer would call it: this is how you do it.

The language gap is the point. Traditional systems often solve problems so elegantly that modern experts later rediscover them and publish papers about them.

Living fences have a long history across tropical farming regions, using a range of hardy plants as boundaries. The cassava version is a particularly interesting member of that family because the barrier material and the staple food are the same species.

It is sustainable without ever using the word. It is efficient without a spreadsheet. It is cheap without a subsidy.

---

12. WHAT THE FENCE TEACHES US

Strip the farming away and there is a bigger idea sitting inside this.

Most of what we call innovation tries to add. A new product, a new layer, a new gadget, a new subscription.

This system does the opposite. It looks at a plant that is already there and asks: what else can this do?

A weed-sized problem, solved with a crop-sized solution.

The best ideas are often not inventions at all. They are reframings. The same object, seen as a different tool.

A stick is not a stick. It is a plant.
A plant is not a plant. It is a wall.
A wall is not a wall. It is a harvest.

Every time you change the question, the object changes with it.

---

13. THE MATH THAT FARMERS DO IN THEIR HEADS

Let's run the numbers the way a smallholder runs them. Not with a calculator. With instinct built over years.

Option one: buy fencing. You pay up front. You pay for transport. You pay for installation, or you pay in your own labor, which is the one resource a small farm never has enough of. Then you pay again when something breaks.

Option two: plant a border from material you already own. You pay in a few hours of work. The cost of the material is close to zero because it is a by-product of the thing you were already doing.

Now add the return.

Option one returns nothing but protection. Option two returns protection plus food plus something to sell plus planting material for next season.

You do not need a degree in economics to see which line goes up faster.

This is the part that gets lost when people call traditional practices simple. They are not simple. They are optimized. The optimization just happened over centuries instead of over a quarter.

---

14. THE STICK IS ALSO THE SEED

Pay attention to a quiet detail here, because it is the engine of the entire system.

In a lot of cassava farming, the harvest produces the next planting. The same plant that gives you the root gives you the stems that become next year's crop.

That is a closed loop.

No seed company. No yearly purchase. No dependence on a distant supplier whose prices change when the weather does.

The farmer who has a cassava field has, built into it, the ability to keep that field going and to extend it. A new border, a new row, a replacement for a gap, a gift to a neighbor. The currency is cuttings, and cuttings are everywhere.

There is something almost ridiculous about how generous the plant is in this respect. It is the opposite of a product. It is more like a living recipe that keeps copying itself for anyone with a knife and some soil.

---

15. THE LEAF THAT FEEDS A COUNTRY

Everyone talks about the root. Hardly anyone talks about the leaf.

In Indonesia, cassava leaves are a real food, cooked into everyday dishes after being properly prepared. Young leaves are boiled, simmered, pounded, mixed with spices and coconut and served with rice. In some households that is a normal weeknight meal, not a novelty.

Cassava leaves are also valued for being nutritious, notably as a source of protein compared with many other leafy greens. In regions where protein is scarce, that matters a lot.

Now put that next to the fence.

A border of cassava is not just a boundary. It is a living vegetable patch. It is a root cellar that hasn't been dug yet. It is a flour source in waiting.

The border does not just protect the pantry. It is the pantry.

And the warning from earlier applies here too: the leaves must be cooked properly. Raw is not the plan. The plant demands technique. Traditional recipes carry that technique inside them, like old software that never needs an update.

---

16. A QUESTION FOR EVERY ENGINEER ON THIS PLATFORM

Imagine you are handed this brief.

Design a perimeter system for a farm. Constraints: near-zero budget, no electricity, no factory components, no specialist installer. It must repair itself. It must scale from one small plot to a large area. It must survive rain, heat and neglect. It must produce something of value while it works.

Now ask yourself honestly: how many engineered solutions pass that brief?

Almost none. Because engineered solutions are usually designed for a different problem: maximum strength, maximum uniformity, maximum control.

Living systems are designed for a different problem: staying alive when conditions are bad.

And a farmer who solves a tight problem with a living system gets a result that a lot of modern design is still trying to imitate under fancy labels like regenerative, adaptive and circular.

The plant is the product. The product is the plan.

---

17. THREE THINGS PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT CASSAVA

Myth one: it is a poor person's crop and nothing more.

Reality: it is a serious commercial crop connected to food, feed and industry across many countries. Poor farmers rely on it because it is reliable, but its economic reach is far wider than subsistence.

Myth two: it is just starch.

Reality: roots are starchy and energy-dense, yes, but the plant as a whole offers more, and the leaves bring protein and micronutrients that the root does not.

Myth three: it is dangerous, so avoid it.

Reality: it is dangerous when prepared carelessly and perfectly safe and nutritious when prepared correctly, which is how it has been eaten for generations. The risk is real, and so is the solution. Respect the process and the plant gives you everything.

Nuance is boring. But nuance is how you avoid both panic and hype.

---

18. THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE LESSON ABOUT TOXICITY

Here is the idea that stuck with me longest while researching this.

We tend to think of toxicity as a flaw, something that makes a crop worse.

For the plant, it is a feature that makes it better at surviving. For the farmer, it is a managed risk that comes with real agronomic advantages: a crop that pests and animals tend to leave alone more often than a tender, sweet alternative would be.

Farmers across history have used this trade-off again and again. Take a plant that defends itself well. Learn how to neutralize the defense in the kitchen. Enjoy a crop that needs less protection in the field.

It is a deal with nature: you handle the chemistry on your side of the table, and the plant handles the defense on its side.

That is not naive farming. That is negotiation.

---

19. WHAT YOU WOULD SEE IF YOU WALKED THE EDGE OF THE FIELD IN A YEAR

Picture the same line of planted sticks across the seasons.

At the start: bare wood, standing like a row of pencils, looking like something a person would throw away.

A few weeks later: tiny shoots break out at the nodes. The row begins to blur at the top.

A few months later: broad, hand-shaped leaves unfold and the line becomes a green curtain, swaying, thick enough to hide what is behind it.

Later still: the plants thicken, toughen and mature. Underground, the swollen roots are developing out of sight.

And at the end: the border you planted as a boundary is the thing you dig up, process and carry home.

Nobody planted a fence and a harvest. They planted a single idea, and time turned it into both.

That is the part that never gets old. The system is patient. It trades speed for compounding. And compounding, whether in money or in plants, beats cleverness almost every time.

---

20. THE HONEST LIMITS

Because credibility matters, let's be straight about what this is not.

It is not a perfect defense against every pest. Determined animals can get through nearly any barrier, and results depend on variety, density, maintenance and what is trying to get in.

It does not eliminate the need for good farming practice. Weed control, soil care, spacing and timing still matter.

It does not remove the safety rules around the plant. Cassava still demands respect in the kitchen.

And it is not magic. It is a trade-off, made intelligently, by people who have decades of local experience about what works on their own land.

The reason it spreads is not hype. The reason is that it is cheap, adaptable and useful in multiple ways at once. That is a much stronger reason than hype ever is.

---

21. THE QUIET GLOBAL SIGNIFICANCE

Climate pressure is making farming harder almost everywhere. Droughts are longer. Soils are tired. Inputs are expensive. Supply chains are fragile.

In that world, a crop that tolerates poor conditions and doubles as infrastructure starts to look less like an old tradition and more like a preview.

Resilient. Local. Low-input. Multi-purpose.

Those four words describe where a lot of serious agricultural thinking is heading. The farmers who plant their field borders with cassava stems got there first, without a conference or a keynote.

There is a lesson in that for every industry: sometimes the future is already operating in a field somewhere, being done by someone who doesn't consider it remarkable.

---

22. WHY YOU CAN'T UNSEE IT NOW

Next time you drink bubble tea, remember the pearls came from a root that carries a chemical defense system.

Next time you see a boring row of green plants along the edge of a field, wonder what it's doing.

Next time you see a pile of old sticks, ask the question that built the whole system: what happens if I put this in the ground?

Because that question, asked by someone, somewhere, generations ago, produced a barrier that grows itself, feeds a family, protects a harvest and ends up in a cup on the other side of the planet.

All from a plant that was built to be left alone.

---

23. THE DETAIL THAT MAKES PEOPLE STOP SCROLLING

Here is the strangest part of the whole story.

Almost nobody who eats cassava ever thinks about how it is grown. It arrives as chips in a bag, pearls in a cup, flour in a bakery, starch in a sauce. The plant is invisible.

But behind every bite is a farmer who made a series of quiet decisions: which stems to keep, where to plant them, how close, which row guards which field, which variety goes to the kitchen and which stays at the edge.

Those decisions are the real technology. They are never patented. They are never branded. They pass from parent to child, from neighbor to neighbor, in a language of gestures and habits that no manual fully captures.

We spend billions chasing new solutions to problems that someone, somewhere, already solved with a knife and a stick.

That is humbling. And it is a reason to pay attention.

Because the next time you meet a problem that looks expensive, ask the Indonesian farmer's question: what is already here that I am not using?

---

24. THE QUESTION THAT STARTS EVERY GOOD IDEA

Every system in this story began with a person looking at a leftover and refusing to see it as waste.

The stems after harvest could have been burned, dumped or ignored. Instead, someone stuck one in the ground and watched what happened. Then someone else copied it. Then a village did. Then a region.

That is how knowledge actually spreads. Not through press releases. Through a neighbor leaning over a fence, noticing that it works, and saying: show me how you did that.

The fence is just the visible part. The invisible part is the habit of curiosity that produced it.

If you remember one habit from this post, make it that one: look at what you are about to throw away and ask what it could become.

---

25. THE ONE-LINE VERSION

If you take only one thing from this, take this:

In Indonesia, some farmers don't build fences. They plant them. And then, eventually, they eat them.

That is the whole story. And it is almost certainly the most efficient perimeter security system ever designed by someone who never called it that.

---

If this made you see a stick differently, you're already smarter than you were five minutes ago.

Now go watch the video. It lasts seconds, but once you know the story behind it, you will not be able to unsee what's happening in it.

Follow for more stories where the boring thing turns out to be genius.

And repost this if you think more people should know that the most ingenious technology on Earth is sometimes just a stick in the dirt.

text:
Good Sunday morning, Patriot 𝕏 friends! 

These pictures are mine from Beaver Creek Chapel in Avon, Colorado. A little stone chapel at the edge of the trees, with the mountains right outside the window.

People talk like God only shows up in the giant places. St. Peter’s. The great cathedrals. The churches that seat thousands and make the news. I love those houses of worship. They are beautiful. They have carried the faith for centuries.

But whenever I am in this small chapel, I remember something I already knew and keep forgetting.
God is not waiting on square footage.

This sanctuary holds about two hundred people, plus a few more in the balcony. There is a wooden altar, a simple cross in front of the trees, a piano, and pews that look like they have heard a lot of quiet prayers. Five congregations share the space. Catholic Mass is offered here. Other Christian services are offered here. Neighbors of different traditions use the same roof. The building is small. The intentions are not.

Scripture never said the Lord only meets us where the architecture is famous. He met people on mountainsides, in upper rooms, by wells, and in little towns nobody planned a pilgrimage around. A chapel in the Rockies is not lesser because it is not Rome. It is another reminder that He comes near. 

I took these pictures because the place means a lot to me.  Not to compare churches. Just to say this out loud that you do not have to be in the biggest sanctuary on earth to be in the presence of God. You can walk up a short set of stone steps, sit in an ordinary pew, look at the trees through the window, and find Him already there.

Have a blessed day, my friends.
#Faith  #Colorado  #Chapel

text:
AI will create more jobs than it kills, McKinsey says. The catch: 11 million Americans may need new careers | Catherina Gioino, Fortune

AI and automation will cut demand for about 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 while growth elsewhere creates about 41 million, according to a new report from the McKinsey Global Institute.

The jobs will exist, the authors argue, but it’s getting workers into them that’s the problem.

“The next decade’s challenge is mobility, not scarcity,” they wrote.

In its base case, about 11 million workers, roughly 7% of the workforce, would need to leave their occupations entirely, with a range of 6 million to 16 million. That’s close to the firm’s 2023 forecast of 12 million career switches by 2030.

Most of those workers would have to jump into an entirely different field, such as retail to healthcare. McKinsey estimates about 770,000 people a year would need to make that kind of switch, roughly 3.6 times the historical average. About 788,000 workers a year made similar moves between 2019 and 2022, during the pandemic, without lasting damage, the report notes.

That would represent a big change for workers, who already move between employers less often than they did in the late 1990s and early 2000s, apart from a brief surge during the pandemic, the report notes.

Credential labor

The shrinking jobs are concentrated in office and administrative support, retail, and transportation, much of it lower-paid work. Lower-wage workers are 7.6 times as likely as higher-wage workers to need a new occupation. Meanwhile, job growth is in healthcare, construction, and management.

Richard Florida, the urbanist and author of The Rise of the Creative Class, told Fortune that shifts like this have happened before. “We used to have most people working in agriculture. Now 1% of the workforce works in agriculture,” he said. “We used to have most people working in manufacturing—50, 60% working in manufacturing. Now 5 to 6% of the workforce works in manufacturing.”

Florida, who was not involved in the McKinsey report, expects displaced service workers to land in what he called “a broad bucket” of wellness work, from fitness and dermatology to Pilates studios. “I think that there will be some displacement,” he said. “But I think this is also the area we’re going to create the most work.” Some of the old service jobs, he said, “become transformed into much higher-paying wellness jobs.”

McKinsey’s data says some of those moves can be difficult for certain workers. Only one in seven displaced workers has a direct path into a growing job, meaning one that needs little retraining and pays at least as much. Nearly half face what the report calls an “unpaved” path, blocked by large skill gaps or credential requirements. About 85% of growing jobs require a credential.

Florida said employers are already changing what they look for. “We used to be hiring really smart people because they’re smart, and then we just watch how they do, up or out,” he said. “Now we’re hiring to replace ourselves. So we’re hiring people who are not just smart but can build the business, work with customers, work with clients, work with others.”

Geography is the other hurdle. About 76% of growing jobs can’t be done remotely, McKinsey found, including work in hospitals, on construction sites, and in data centers.

Florida’s research has long tracked how different kinds of work settle in different places. “There’s manual work, which is like farm work or factory work, and that tends to be distributed almost ubiquitously over space,” he said. “Then there’s cognitive work, which tends to concentrate in big cities.”

Cities take the lead

He said people are already willing to move for opportunity, even to places whose politics they dislike. He pointed to Canadians moving from Toronto to Miami. “They don’t necessarily like political conservatism. They don’t necessarily like Donald Trump,” he said. “But they like that Miami is a nice place to live and offers low taxes and has a lot of economic opportunity.”

People moving to Nashville, where he now teaches, tell him “it’s good to live in a blue city in a red state. I pay less taxes. I can still live in a kind of interesting city, but I saved a huge percent of my income.”

When he wrote The Rise of the Creative Class in 2002, Florida said he didn’t foresee how technology would let people spread out. “I certainly didn’t talk about the rise of AI and AI technology and the way it would allow people to distribute.”

Cities are also trying to pull talent in by building universities. Citadel founder Ken Griffin, who moved the hedge fund from Chicago to Miami in 2022, committed $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University on Sept. 30. Of that, $2 billion will fund a new Miami campus, which plans to enroll its first students in 2028. Vanderbilt is building a graduate campus in West Palm Beach focused on business, AI, and data science, with $50 million from developer Stephen Ross leading the fundraising.

Florida, who joined Vanderbilt’s faculty this fall, said wealthy people who moved to South Florida first “figured out they didn’t have to bring their companies with them. They could just bring their boats and their family office.” Griffin, he said, “realized that it has to be a talent anchor.”

BREAKING: The Iranian Army, not the Revolutionary Guard, says it is extending the range of its missiles because the Americans are staying further away from the coast.

Spokesperson Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia gave the interview to Fars on Sunday. The quote cited by Iran Observer is genuine: they concluded during wartime that they needed to increase range, and they have moved in that direction. Reuters, Mehr, WANA, and Xinhua confirm this. It is not a test; it is an intention.

The 1,000-kilometer figure is not a new ceiling for the strategic program. Akraminia notes that the enemy now operates up to about 1,000 kilometers from the shore, so the Army's missiles must be able to reach that distance. He speaks of speed and precision for all Army missiles. Ground force missiles have struck bases in Kuwait; Navy cruise missiles have struck ships. These are the systems they want to extend.

The distinction from the headline lies in the institution involved. Until now, long-range missiles belonged to the Revolutionary Guard, while the Army handled coastal defense and naval operations. If the Artesh (regular Army) extends its reach beyond 1,000 kilometers, it overlaps with the IRGC's domain. This does not replace the self-imposed 2,000-kilometer limit announced for years regarding ballistic missiles; rather, it bypasses that limit within the naval sector.

The signal is aimed at aircraft carriers, not Washington. A carrier strike group typically positions itself just beyond the old range of coastal missiles. Akraminia is shifting the goalposts to demonstrate that distance no longer offers protection. Bessent states that the navy and air force have been destroyed and missile stockpiles depleted. Tehran responds with a missile, not a ship.

Nothing in the interview shows a new missile on the launch rail. It shows that the lesson of the 40-day war, which ended on April 8, was the thrashing they took. The next test, if it comes, will be the real proof. Until then, it is just doctrine read aloud.

If the Islamic Republic could vote, whom would it choose: Benjamin Netanyahu or Donald Trump? It sounds like an abstract problem, but the choice facing Tehran is the same one Citizen Change posed to American voters in 2004: “Vote or Die.”

With the U.S. blockade plunging Iran into an ever-deepening economic crisis, Tehran must break the status quo. The question is when. Escalating before the Israeli election and the midterms would send the markets into an inconvenient panic and Israeli jets to Tehran. Any conversation outside of security would be quickly stifled, burying some of Netanyahu’s other indiscretions while bringing gas prices and Trump’s failures to the front of American voters’ minds on November 3. A war before October 27 is a vote for Bibi and against Trump.

Tehran, reluctant to boost Netanyahu’s security credentials, could wait until both elections are over, but that is casting a vote for Trump.

Observant readers will notice that there is a gap between the two trips to the ballot box. Tehran has a single week, between October 27 and November 3, in which it can launch a war without helping either candidate.

There is also the risk that, unlike winter, election season makes war more likely. Trump is currently holding back to give Republicans a chance of holding the Senate, telling reporters the war will be brought to a conclusion “right after the midterms.” While I struggle to imagine a fate worse than the hell on earth Trump has already threatened to unleash multiple times, if Iran extinguishes whatever electoral hopes are constraining the president, the response is unlikely to be the controlled escalation Tehran may be hoping for.

Despite declaring at the United Nations that “the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions,” President Masoud Pezeshkian reportedly approached Steve Witkoff, Trump’s special envoy, with an Iranian compromise the same day. Like an Iranian moderate, an Iranian compromise exists mainly by comparison.

The offer was essentially identical to the memorandum of understanding: Iran would open the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for sanctions relief and the unfreezing of assets, with the fig leaf that maybe, perhaps, if the U.S. is on its best behavior, Iran might let nuclear inspectors into the country, potentially. Unsurprisingly, Nazi Germany offering to sell France back in 1945 would not have been a tempting offer.

Despite his past enthusiasm for such terms, Vice President JD Vance did not jump at the offer, and Trump dismissed it out of hand, though Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is still in denial, insisting no formal rejection has been conveyed. The very act of negotiating is an indicator of desperation rather than deradicalization, brought on by the blockade, tightening sanctions and isolation from regional states that have grown sick of Iranian antics. According to Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and envoy, “The U.S. has achieved greater impact in a matter of weeks than during the lengthier campaigns commenced from 2010.”

But while the attempted outreach indicates desperation on the part of Araghchi and Pezeshkian, the unchanged terms suggest that while Tehran burns, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Ahmad Vahidi is still fiddling, confident he can endure the economic pain and outlast American patience.

Trump’s dwindling patience may be getting a refill. According to JPMorgan, oil traffic is back to 98 percent of prewar levels, an impressive accomplishment by the U.S. Navy in only four months, all the more so given how erratic those months have been. Even the apparent glimmer of hope from the Houthis has not materialized. Though they seized the coastline overlooking the Bab al-Mandab last month, they have yet to effectively close the strait, and according to Yemen’s armed forces, they lost nearly 3,000 killed and wounded in four days. Saudi Arabia is now preparing a counteroffensive that could mobilize more than 100,000 Yemeni troops under Saudi air cover. Washington has twice declined Riyadh’s request to join, though U.S. officials say that could change if the operation falters.

The truth is Iran has a larger problem than timing: its vote doesn’t matter. Trump still has months before a Democratic-controlled Congress could begin impeachment proceedings, and even while trapped in endless inquiries, he still holds the power over the military and foreign policy. Meanwhile, whoever becomes the next Israeli prime minister, in the increasingly unlikely event the election produces a definitive outcome at all, Jerusalem is not going to turn pro-Tehran. No matter who they vote for, nothing will change in time for Iran to survive.

🔴WAR ON TERRORISM: IRAN 🇮🇷🔴/Jerusalem Post / 

US remains 'hell-bent' on preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, says Hegseth

The US defense secretary said Trump would have every military option available, maintained that Washington controls the Strait of Hormuz, and acknowledged that Iran is attempting to rebuild its damag

By IDAN KWELLER

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth warned Iran that US President Donald Trump remains determined to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons, cautioning that Tehran must choose between relinquishing its nuclear ambitions and facing further American action.

Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Hegseth also declined to confirm whether the United States intends to deploy a third aircraft carrier to the region, saying his responsibility is to ensure that Trump retains the widest possible range of military options.

Asked directly whether three aircraft carriers would be deployed, Hegseth replied: “It’s a fair question, but I will never answer it.”

“I’d say maximizing the decision space for the commander in chief at any point is my job, while also recognizing the way we balance global demands as a force with global responsibilities,” he explained.

“So the president’s going to have options. Let’s put it that way, and I’ll leave it there.”

‘Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon’

Hegseth delivered his strongest warning when asked to clarify the administration’s message to Tehran.

“Well, the message is very simple: Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

“President Trump is hell-bent and determined to ensure that they do not. They will not. If they want to blink and think that he doesn’t mean it, it would be to their detriment.”

He added that Iran had reached a decision point.

“So now’s a moment where they can decide to give it up the way that they should, without any leverage that they have, or it may have to happen the hard way.”

Earlier in the exchange, Hegseth was asked whether he expected military operations to conclude before the end of the year. He declined to commit to a timetable, deferring the decision to Trump.

He nevertheless contrasted the administration’s approach with previous American military campaigns that, he said, had continued for years or decades without clearly defined objectives or an identifiable end state.

“As we’ve stated from the beginning, Iran will never have a nuclear bomb. Full stop. That is a vital national interest of the United States of America,” Hegseth said, citing Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.

He stressed that Trump would not allow operations to continue unnecessarily, arguing that the administration understands its mission and has the capabilities required to accomplish it.
Hegseth acknowledges Iranian efforts to rebuild missile capabilities

Asked whether Washington had evidence that Iran was attempting to reconstitute its missile capabilities and launchers, Hegseth said the United States was monitoring developments in real time.

He acknowledged that Tehran would attempt to rebuild its military infrastructure but maintained that the damage inflicted during Operation Epic Fury had severely complicated those efforts.

“Think of it this way, their Raytheons, their Boeings, their Lockheeds, their Northrop Grummans are what was destroyed in Epic Fury,” he said, referring to the Iranian equivalents of major American defense manufacturers.

“So they’re going to attempt to reconstitute, and they’re a terror state.

So they’re going to always attempt to reconstitute, but when you’ve been so destroyed and degraded the way that they have, it’s a very slow process, a very frustrating process, and we see that, and we understand that.”

Hegseth argued that the extent of the damage to Iran’s defense industrial base, economy, and ability to rebuild would continue to constrain Tehran’s military options.

‘They don’t control the Strait of Hormuz, we do’

The defense secretary also emphasized American control over the Strait of Hormuz, describing the US blockade as a central component of Washington’s pressure campaign against Iran.

“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it. We do,” Hegseth said.

“Our blockade has been ironclad, and we’re running almost at pre-war levels every single night through that,” he added, referring to maritime throughput.

Hegseth asserted that Iran’s naval and air capabilities had been so extensively degraded that it could no longer effectively challenge American dominance over the strategic waterway.

“It’s pretty tough for them to control the Strait of Hormuz when they don’t have a navy.

They don’t have fast boats, and they’ve got no air force,” he said.

“And then we’ve done such incredible damage to their ability to see and sense the Strait of Hormuz. We control it. We dominate it in both an asymmetric and a conventional sense.”

He added that Washington was capable of maintaining the blockade for as long as necessary and adapting its implementation according to operational requirements.

“The longer we hold the blockade, and we can hold it as long as we need to.

Trust me, we can adapt that as necessary,” he said, arguing that the pressure would further restrict Tehran’s remaining options.

Asked whether the conflict could ultimately have a military solution, Hegseth said it could be resolved in multiple ways and maintained that Trump had repeatedly offered Iran an opportunity to reach an agreement through negotiations.

“The president has given Iran every opportunity to do it at the table,” he said.

However, he reiterated that the combination of American military strikes and the continuing blockade had left Washington in a strong position.

“Iran ought to make the right choice. If they don’t, the president’s going to have all the options he needs on the table,” Hegseth concluded.

text:
Adults start at 30? Which country? This is a combination of so many things. If a grown-up university student wants to be an adult at 30, you sincerely see problems. 

For everyone that went to Campus they know that hunger is real, but without responding with emotions and seperating government aside, we have so many things to attend to. 

First, university education is expensive, not affordable for people with low incomes, and this makes access discriminatory. So, in response to this crisis, to still make sure their children must also study, some serious parents, guardians, and students who accept their situation always have three or four alternatives.

1. Go to a university in their districts or home locations. There, you can commute from home.

2. Branch to diploma-awarding institutions if they can't afford a degree and climb gradually. Many offer government schemes, have accommodation, and affordable meals

3. Keep the student out for a year or two while working to raise at least some substansive amount of money before they can join, or, better still, 

4. Enrol in weekend courses and remain home while working or doing some projects. Here, you save yourself from hunger and from living a life you cannot afford. 

Second issue.  Those who want adulthood at 30 know how to spend on campus and live beyond their means. Many of them forced themselves to go to expensive institutions because of peer pressure, and in the end the parents get stuck—these same people like living beyond their means. Give them the money they're asking for; tomorrow you won't find it. Because they chose to be babies in their 20s, they know how to spend more than they can manage. 

Lastly, what the government needs to urgently improve is student welfare. Private students, whether poor or better off, come ready to plan for their stay. Government students take a long time to get their allowance. These are among the groups dying with hunger. 

So yes, this is a reality, but we are all answerable. Discuss university education as a family and think about how you will manage the three or five years. Don't let the student choose, or don't follow the bandwagon. Choose what you can afford and sustain so that we can face off with other unavoidable circumstances, like abrupt changes in income, like loss of jobs, collapse of business, sickness of a sponsor. 

Finally, nurture responsibility; someone who thinks she is a baby, even at 30, will be the same. She can't afford food, but wait until her birthday; she will spend. Some can blow all the money you sent them on parties, to wake up the next day with nothing to eat. 

As for the government, they have a lot. I can't write much because it's what they know. What I have written is what I, as a parent or student, can work on.

text:
Please, someone help this mother and her baby.

The mother is mentally challenged. The baby is innocent and completely clueless about the circumstances into which he or she was born.

They have no home. They sleep outside. They struggle to find food. They wake up each morning with nothing guaranteed except another day of trying to survive.

Sometimes they eat whatever they can find. Sometimes they sleep wherever darkness finds them.

And the baby knows nothing about poverty, mental illness or the cruelty of the streets. All this child knows is that they need warmth, food, safety and a mother's arms.

I keep asking myself: How can we see a mother and an innocent child living like this and simply walk away?

The mother may not be in a position to save herself. That is precisely why society must step in.

This baby did not choose the street. This mother did not choose to lose her ability to care for herself.

Let us not wait for tragedy before we act.

We need to get this child off the streets. We need to find the mother a safe place, get them food, clothing, medical and psychosocial support, and connect them with people who can ensure they are protected.

If you know where they are, if you can offer shelter, food, professional help or any form of support, please come forward.

Let us be the people this child remembers, even if they never know our names.

A child should not have to grow up believing that the street is home.

Please, let us save this baby.

text:
RHAPSODY OF REALITIES TEEVO

PASTOR CHRIS OYAKHILOME 

SUNDAY, 4TH OCTOBER 2026

BECOME VISIONARY

(Make A Difference In The World)

TO THE BIBLE - Matthew 5:14 KJV
“Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."

LET’S  TALK
Imagine a world where everyone asked, “How can I make a difference today?” What a beautiful place it would be! Often, we think success is about what we can gain, but true success is measured by what we give. It’s about leaving the world better than we found it. The world needs visionaries: young people who will step out from the crowd, find a need, and reach out to meet that need. That’s one of the principles of success—when you’re challenged to make things better than the way you met them. 

Instead of being the one asking for help and waiting for others to give to you, you should become the helper! Become the one to  meet other people’s needs.  Be the blesser and the  giver, for that’s your calling.  The Bible shows us that Joseph stood out in his day and saved the entire  nation  of  Egypt from starvation  during a time of famine  (Genesis  41:55). Think  about your school, your group of friends, or your community; maybe someone is being bullied, struggling with school, or just needs a friend; you don’t have to solve the world’s problems first; you can start small.

This is your set time to make a difference in your world. The world ought to be a better place because you came. And you know what? It begins with being passionate about a God-idea and having the courage to implement that idea once you receive it from God. It doesn’t matter how small the idea may seem; once you have it, run with it. Before long, God will expand your vision and increase your inspiration! He’ll grant you the motivation and the ability to conceive and execute more ideas that’ll impact the world and make it a better place. Wake up to that calling today. Praise God! 

GO DEEPER

Proverbs 11:24-25 There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. [25] The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.

PRAY

Dear Heavenly Father, I thank you for giving me the inspiration, motivation and ability to conceive and execute divine ideas that’ll make the world a better place. I recognise that this is my season and set time to make a difference in the world; therefore, by the power of the Spirit, I’m impacting the world with the investment of my personality! Thank you for making me a blesser and a giver, in Jesus’ Name. Amen.

DAILY BIBLE READING

ONE YEAR
Philippians 2:1-18, Isaiah 13-14

TWO YEAR 
John 3:9-21, 1 Kings 8

ACT

Look around your immediate environment: your home, your school, your neighbourhood; identify one problem, big or small, and take a step towards solving it. Offer help, share an idea, or lend a hand.

✍️MY NOTES
